blocks.x: Can you give me some information on when you were born and where around town you were brought up?

I was born December the 6th, 1910, somewhere on Tulane Avenue. My father's memory is a little hazy now because he's very near 78. But it's somewhere around Tulane and Miro, I think. And I lived mostly around Bank Street. You might say the third ward, which took in Durgin Wall Street. And then later on I moved out in the fourth ward, which took in Lakeview. This was when I was about 12 years old.
There's someone near the channel now, don't you? There's someone near the Irish channel?
Well, at the time that I was coming up, Charlie, no, I don't believe that that was the Irish channel around that section. The Irish channel was more in the uptown section.
But you mean now, don't you live around close to the channel?
Oh, yes. That's right. Now, for the past 35 years, I've been living uptown, very close to the original Irish channel.
Okay. How about a little bit on where you learned how to play piano and what extent of formal training you had, and maybe how you first got interested in jazz piano?

Well, I guess, Charlie, I had a desire to play music ever from the time that I could remember myself, although I don't say that I was a child prodigy because I don't remember playing when I was two years old or a year and a half old. But when I was about six or seven, I think I played drums when I was at school, a little school band. And then later on, my mother, who played piano, a little bit, who did not read very much, but she knew enough to be able to encourage me. And it used to fascinate me just to sit down and watch her play and listen to her play little pieces. So she gave me a lot of encouragement. And, in fact, she told me that she wanted me to start taking some private lessons after she had already given me some ideas about the scale and the notes and so forth, which I had quite an advantage when I began taking.
Did you study privately for any great length of time, or did you more or less go off on your own with listening to pianists about town or what?

Well, I started with this lady by the name of Mrs. Essett. How do you spell that? A-S-E-T-T. And she was a very wonderful person who had the patience of a saint because I did not want to study the sort of things that she was giving me. And she insisted that I should learn more of the rudiments of the basic things, you know, that you had to know. But it seemed like everywhere I'd come out I'd listen to the old player piano rolls and the old Edison phonographs in those days, you know, playing the old Dixieland records and listening to the old jazz bands march up and down the street and all that sort of thing. And, well, everywhere I turned around I mean I just heard jazz music. And of course in those days it was more commonly referred to as ragtime, you know. Right. Right. A lot of the people didn't say, well do you play jazz? Because I know that when I was going to my teacher I told her, I said, oh, I said, you know, I love to play some of those ragtime tunes that I hear on the player piano. And she says, well, she said, that'll come in time, you know. I said, yeah, but that's just it. I says, I don't want to wait. I says, I'd like to play now. So she had a hard time keeping me from digging into some of these ragtime tunes that were out at the time, like Maple Leaf Rag and some of the other tunes, Spaghetti Rag, and well, you know, just a couple, name a few.
Were there any particular bands or specific musicians who were especially encouraging when you were just trying to get into the jazz or if you will ragtime playing?

Right. There were no specific musicians, Charlie, in the early period because if you will figure this, that I started taking lessons when I was about eight or nine years old. And, of course, that's pretty young, you know, especially when you go back into those old days and people, the way they were, you know, kind of strict, you didn't get much chance to get out too much. Right. I didn't meet too many musicians. I wasn't around too many musicians. But there was one man, his name was Edward Bordeaux. I have never mentioned this man's name prior to any other interviews, Charlie, and it's the first time that I have ever really gave this any real thought when you, you know, when you asked me did I ever meet any other musicians. And this man was really not a professional but played ragtime very fluently. And, you know, he used to come around the house and he couldn't play without the music. And he'd come with a rag, a roll of music, you know, wrapped up, you know, into his home and he'd sit there and he'd bring out these rags, you know, and he'd start playing chicken reel rag and, oh, good gravy rag. And I'd just go crazy to just listen to him play these rags. And he played them very, very mechanical and with not too much relaxation. But it was really one of the probably the oiliest influences that I had.
Would you remember how you spelled his name, Bordeaux, you said?

Yes, he was a very good friend of the families. And his name was Edward Bordeaux, which was a French name, and I think the name was B-O-R-D-E-A-U-X. When did you first start playing professionally? Well, now there's a little gap in between, Charlie, that when I hit around ten years old, well, I actually took about a year, I guess, of private lessons. And then when I hit this period of about ten and a half to eleven years old, I kind of got disinterested. And we moved away from the Bank Street area out into Lakeview. And this brought me into close contact with an uncle of mine by the name of Dewey Schmid, who used to be an old vaudeville entertainer. Dewey Schmid. Dewey Schmid. But his stage name was Wilbur Leroy, L-E-R-O-Y. And he was quite a character who really, really loved good blues, you know, and he faked piano a little bit, you know. And every chance he'd get, he'd come around and he'd start showing me how to fake the left hand, you know. He'd say, why don't you do it this way, Omin, instead of doing it the way you're doing it right now, you know. And my mother would hear me playing this left hand the way he was telling me how to do it, you know. She'd come running and, you know, telling me, don't play like that, don't play like that. As soon as she'd go out and get out of the way, I'd start playing it again.
Was that more or less a ragtime bass you were using there, or was it?

Well, I wouldn't exactly say that it was a ragtime bass because it was sort of a real low-down, I'd say more of a blues honky-tonk style of bass that he used. It was something that the piano players used to use a lot, you know. They used that one, two, three, four, boom, you know. They'd get that sort of little one, two, three, one, two, three, four, one, you know, and then they'd sort of get that little skip beat in between, which was really a real good beat. In fact, I wouldn't classify it as a real ragtime beat. I think it was more of a jazz beat.
Well, now, is this how you kind of eased in professionally? Well, yes, I would. Right.

This uncle started easing me in professionally because he gave me a lot of encouragement. And, in fact, when I was about twelve years old he took me to a neighborhood show, a neighborhood theater with him. You know, there was the days when they had silent pictures and they used to have an old piano player down in the pit. And then after the picture was over, well, they had a little vaudeville entertainment. Well, this was real great in those days, you know. So the piano player didn't show up. So my uncle and his partner were stuck for a piano player. So my uncle told me, he says, Oman, you think you can play a couple of tunes for us? So, gee, I started shaking, you know, and I said, well, I'll try, you know. So I got in there and I started faking, how come you do me like you do, do, do, and there'll be some changes made or something else. I forget just what couple of tunes that they did. Real, real old time vaudeville stuff, you know.
Did they see you accompanying them or was this your spot or what? No, I didn't have a feature spot.

I was just accompanying them. They were singing, you know, and I was following along. But I got such a big kick out of this that really this was probably one of the greatest thrills in my life. And it really wound up real bad for me because after the theater closed that night, my uncle took me to a wine place. And this was in the days of prohibition, you know. And they had to knock it, you know, and get inside. And they proceeded to giving me this homemade wine. By the time I got home, I was really some sick boy. My uncle didn't come around the house for about a month after that.

It's quite an initiation. Yeah, it was almost the end of my career. Okay. Well, what band did you get to playing with? Well, let's say this, what kind of work did you do in those days? Did you get pretty quickly into the kind of work where you could play ragtime and jazz? Or did you do a lot of commercial work? Or why did you play music professionally full time or what? Can you kind of set that up for me?

I would say that it was kind of commercial in the very beginning because we had little bands like the kids do today. They get together in the homes, you know, and they get little arrangements, you know. They were already writing little specialized arrangements like on college songs, you know, collegiate, collegiate, yes, we're all collegiate, and yes, that's my baby, and all those sort of tunes, Charleston and those things were beginning to come out. And they had little arrangements on them, and of course most of the kids read a little bit, and we'd sit down and we'd practice these things, you know. And I would say that it more or less was, you'd say, kind of commercial because there were really no real jazz musicians mixed up in this except the fact that we were trying to play and get started. And I played a few jobs like that. And then I think about the first real job professionally that I ever had. I've often referred to another place, which I will tell you about later, but I think this first job that I had was in a neighborhood theater. They called for three pieces, violin, piano, and drums. And of course our job was to play for the silent movies because they had no sound, you know. And this was at a theater called the St. Maurice Avenue Theater, which I think is no longer in existence now. Was that below the bridge?
It was below the bridge, yes.

And I used to ride all the way from Lakeview to St. Maurice Avenue on a streetcar. And we got the big salary of a dollar a piece a night. But of course in those days, you know, a dollar was pretty good, you know. And for a couple of kids, I mean, it looked real good to us. And I guess money was always just secondary, Charlie, if you really loved the music the way we did in those days. I mean, I know it was always that way with me. If I had enough money to navigate on, and I mean, I'd go on jobs and wouldn't even ask, what is it going to pay? Right. All I wanted to know is where was it, how long was it going to be, and all that sort of thing. It's just a little different then. I don't think it's quite that way now. No.
You say there were no other of the second generation jazz musicians in this young group that you led with? Not at that time.

Not at that time. I had not yet come in contact with anyone. This came later, after I played at this little theater down here. There was a drummer, who I must confess that my memory is just failing me a little bit at this point here, who was working at the Furn Dance Hall. And he met my father and told my father, he said, there is a very good position open at a dance hall. He says, and it would pay Ormond $25 or $30 a week. Well, I was only 14 years old at the time. And when he told me that, I said, gee, I said, I'd love to do it. So they said it would be from eight to one. So when I told my mother about it, she liked to flip, you know, going to work in a dance hall. Fourteen years old, I had just gone in long pants, because you know, in those days we used to wear short pants until we were 12, 13 years old. And I had just gone in the long pants. But my mother finally consented to let me go to work under one condition. My uncle, the brother of Durschmeed, his name was George Schmeed, which was another brother of my mother's. He was the night policeman down on Canal Street. And everybody knew him. He was about 6'2 and weighed about 350 pounds. And everybody knew him. They called him Smith or Schmeed or I don't know what they had, Corporal. They had all kind of names for him. So my mother says, well, as long as your Uncle George sees you home in the morning time, it's all right. So when it would come time to me to...

get off, my uncle would pass around the fern and he would see that I got on a streetcar and got home. So this was the only way that I was able to start playing at such an early age, especially in a place like a dance hall.
Right. Did all this extracurricular activity bump into your schooling and did you have to quit

or did you carry on? Well, that's right. I gave up. I was going to Warren Eastern High School at the time and found out that I couldn't quite make it. So I said, well, I knew right then and there, I said, there's only one thing for me, that's music. I had no desire to learn anything else but just to play music. Now you asked me about some musicians. Here was a place where I began meeting the old Real Dixieland musicians. For instance, we had a drummer playing there by the name, he replaced the fellow that really got me the job, was Von Gammon.
Yeah.

Von Gammon then became leader and they had, let's see, they had Harry Shields, who was a brother of Larry Shields playing in the band. And we had an old banjo player by the name of Buzzy Willards, who was very good, and a trumpet player by the name of Bill Gillum, and a clarinet player by the name of Bill Bourgeois. Well, of course, Bill is still active today.
Yeah.

Right. I said, I said, Harry Shields was playing clarinet. Bill replaced Harry later on. That's right. Now, the point is this, Charlie, that in this place, all the musicians used to drop in, you see, because it was a meeting place. Shawky used to stop in there. Fasola. Fasola was about, well, when I was playing there, Fasola was a little younger than me. And you talk about something funny. He used to come around in short pants. And he weighed about, he weighed about 200 pounds with short pants and a cap. There must have been a picture. A picture is right. And he played just as wonderful then as he did later on. And, um, and...
I'm sorry, before you go on, did you mention the name of this place?
The Fern. The Fern. It was called The Fern Dance Hall. And it was on Canal Street? It was on, uh, it was on Iverville one time, and then it was also on Burgundy at one time.
Okay, thank you. Okay, now, did you want to comment any further on this is how you got into the, the...

This was the real beginning of jazz for me, as far as really jazz was concerned, because I'll never forget, I went there with a couple of pieces of music, you know, that I'd had. When I got there, Von Gammon, the leader of the band, says, what are you doing with that, homin? I said, well, I thought I might need it. He says, just take one look around. He says, do you think you'd be able to see it? I says, no, I don't think so. So Harry Shields told me, he says, don't worry, he says, I'll call the chords out to you, you know. And this is the way I learned all the Dixieland tunes, Charlie, because they'd call out jazz me blues, and I'd say, well, I don't know that. I never played it before in my life. They said, don't worry about it, we'll call the chords out to you, you see. So after about two or three nights, you'd get familiar with the tune, you know. Right. Or they'd play That's A Plenty, or jazz band ball, or Millen Boyd Joy. Is that a, the big thing in those days was a four-minute slow drag, you know. Everybody got a dime ticket or a nickel ticket. I just don't remember what they used to charge them. And this was a big dance for the fellas that would come in, because they'd give them a four-minute dance for one ticket, you see. And they'd say, the next dance is going to be a four-minute slow drag. And usually they'd play tin rule blues, which was a real good blues. And of course, this is the way that I practically learned all of the Dixieland tunes, right, right in that Fern dance hall.

I just want to get one more thing on the biography before we go on. After you started with this group at the Fern, was it? Yeah. Did you do mostly after that single work? I've known you always as a single since I was first a jazz fan. Did you have any other gigs that you think were especially worthy of note, either with a group or as a single, that were important to you as you developed in your career?

Not as a single, Charlie, because I worked with groups there. I went from the Fern dance hall over to a little nightclub or cabaret, they call it in those days, called the Valencia, where the Hilton Inn is supposed to go up today on Bourbon Street. And I worked there with a little three-piece group with Chink Morton's son, who played banjo, and Eddie Miller, who played alto sax in those days. And we had a little three-piece outfit. And, well, from there I went to various places. I don't know if I can get them just in order, but I worked at the Silver Slipper, which later, in later years, became known as the Dream Room, and now the Father's Mustache. But in those days, the Silver Slipper nightclub was really one of the real swing places in the city. And I worked there with a very fine musician by the name of Sidney Arden. Sidney Arden, you know, wrote Upper Lazy River. And, of course, Hoagie Carmichael collaborated with Sidney on this tune. Well, naturally, I mean, very few people ever refer to the tune as Sidney's. They always say Hoagie's tune. Well, of course, actually, and not to take any credit away from Hoagie, the tune originally was, from what I can understand, and I quote other musicians, that Sidney had this tune for quite a while, but it was under a different title. I won't quote the title because the title was not very appropriate. Okay. Did you do much out-of-town work? Did you go on the road much? Not very much, Charlie. I was always more or less a homebody guy who couldn't get out of town very much. I went over to the Gulf Coast once when, oh, I forget the name of the play, I believe it was the Hotel Markham. I don't know if that hotel is still in existence. I think it is, yeah. And they had a little band over there. Eddie Miller sent for me. He was playing over there. I went over there, stayed over there about a week, and got so homesick, I said, Eddie, I can't stand this old way. I said, I want to go back to New Orleans.

This seems to be something that's always struck me as sort of almost a tradition among New Orleans musicians, the reluctance to leave town. I guess Chicago, almost forced out because of the closing of Storyville, and then we know on the current pop charts, our hurt, you know, for a long time resisted leaving town, and so did Pete Fountain. Have you ever thought about this? Why is that there's such a reluctance on the part of major talents, such as yourself, to leave town? It seems like there are big markets elsewhere. There's lots of money. There's recognition and stardom that's not exactly attainable here. Have you ever given any thought as to why, generally,

Orleanians seem hesitant about going on the road? Well, I would imagine that it is the glamorous atmosphere that New Orleans offers, not money-wise, but certainly it has plenty of atmosphere, and if you're born here, you know what it is. It's just as you say, do you know what it means to miss New Orleans? Well, this is very true, and if you have ever been away for a while, why do you get this urge to come back? And, of course, I was always, as I said, sort of a guy that was stuck close to home, and, well, one time my uncle wanted me to go to New York, and my mother liked to have a fit because he was trying to talk me in the game, going to New York, and I think this sort of put a sort of damper on things, too. Mm-hmm. Well, kept sound. All right.
You said before that there were no specific pianists who influenced you when you came up. Generally speaking, what pianists would influence your style, do you think?

Well, I heard pianists all around me, but many of the good pianists, such as Jelly Roll, had already gone. As you say, why did some of these musicians hate to leave? Well, they all hated to leave, I guess, but more or less the musicians who felt that they wanted to make something, or make a name, or make money, they couldn't do it in the Walls. They had to leave. And, of course, Jelly Roll was gone, Spencer Williams was gone, Clarence Williams, King Oliver, all the real greats struck out sooner or later. And then, of course, the original Dixieland Jazz Band had already begun, you know, to make history with Nicola Rocca and Harry Shields and all those boys. And they all left New Orleans, Tom Brown, every one of them. Tom Brown ran into some bad luck up there and so forth and so on. But more or less, as you say, the musicians were reluctant to leave. Now, getting back to the pianist, many of the good pianists had already gone. Like I say, Jelly Roll Morton was not around. I never did get to know Steve Lewis, who Dr. Souchon tells me was very, very good. And I had a resort to listening to a lot of player piano roles, listening to Jelly Roll on some of the player roles, listening to the old, some of the old timers like Scott Joplin and the old ragtime piano players, and then listening to the phonograph recordings. And I did hear a few snatches of some good piano here and there. But to tell you the truth, Charlie, the real good pianists were not here. There were very, very few. The old timers spoke of a piano player by the name of Leonard Beisdorfer, who was a brother to Johnny Beisdorfer. And they said that he was excellent, but I never did get to meet him.
Well, certainly your piano style goes beyond the ragtime realm. What have any other pianists of the swing era or the modern era influence your playing as it's constituted today?

I think that the first real impact that hit me, when I say impact, I was already going under the influence of the old timers like Jelly Roll and the ragtime pianists. And I had one pianist around here by the name of Buzzy Williams, who was very, very excellent, and he gave me a lot of encouragement and a lot of help. But getting back to the other pianists, I would say that the first one that really had a terrific impact on me was Earl Hines. I think that he did more to revolutionize my style of playing probably than any other pianist that I know of. And then came Jess Stacy, who played in the big band with Goodman, and of course Teddy Wilson, who I think was simply superb. And of course then I wouldn't leave out good old Fats Wally. Fats had a terrific influence on me too in those days. And I see these pianists began to have an influence on me, but it was only after I had been playing for many years.
Did you take up, were you taken up much by Art Tatum's style?
Very much. Oh yes, yes, definitely with Art Tatum. I was definitely taken up with him. I first heard him I think around 36 or 37, something like that.
Who do you like or do you have any taste for the modern jazz pianists of today? Do you find any kinship with them in particular?

Oh, definitely Charlie, definitely. I follow the pianists, I guess, practically all of them. I've lost track of some of the modern ones because they're coming so fast these days that I just can hardly keep up with them. But I've kept up with most of them and I just think that they're just the greatest. Like for instance, I think George Shearing is superb. I think Amma Jamal is. I think Errol Garner in his own way. I mean a lot of people just don't particularly care for him, but I think he's real great. And, well, for instance, even today, Bill Evans, I've heard some of his recordings and my God, I just think they're terrific. I think he has a wonderful feeling for jazz.

That's kind of brings us into my next point very naturally. You're known internationally, basically, as a ragtime pianist. Do you think that this is an apt description of your style? I'm sure it limits your range to call you a ragtime pianist. What do you think of the tag personally, though?

Yes, I think the tag ragtime is sort of put me in a certain category that has been hard for me to overcome from lots of directions. The people who traditionally like ragtime don't like to hear me play anything else. And, of course, I don't play in a strict progressive sense. That's okay. But I would say that just saying that I'm a ragtime piano player, while I feel very flattered to have been included in this category with many of the real ragtime greats, I think I went a little beyond that because I didn't stop there. In other words, I feel this way, that if you're a pianist, you play piano. If you're a musician, you play music. For instance, I think Will Hines could probably play ragtime if he wanted to. I think Teddy Wilson could probably play ragtime. He may not be really a real traditionalist, but I think that they could play ragtime if they really wanted to. And I think that they've gone beyond that and they've gone through different phases.

Certainly, I don't see any harm in keeping up with some of the things that are going on. I think it's kind of ironic that you say the people who like to hear you play ragtime like little else, and it must cause a problem on a job, because most people don't come to the night to the average cocktail lounge to hear ragtime, which is a problem. That's right. Would you like to play more ragtime in the cocktail work where you're limited to playing very little of it? You often feel the urge to play more, even though it's incompatible with the kind of mild surroundings of a cocktail lounge.

Well, it's very funny, Charlie, that you ask me that, because lots of times I did feel as though I was being done an injustice. When I was at the height of my build-up as a Dixieland pianist and as a ragtime pianist, I was not able to really play this kind of music as I wanted to. And I was hoping, this was about, I guess, say maybe 10, 15 years ago, that I could have been working in places where I could have really just maybe stuck to this particular type of music and either became known as one type of pianist or another. But as you said, it is very difficult because, as you know, when you're working in a public place, you get all types of people, all tastes of music, and you sort of have to go along with the public. I don't have to tell you that. You know, you're playing right now with a little group, and you all go along sort of with the public. I mean, if they want a particular thing, well, you play it for them. And this is what I try to do. Now, I don't know if I would be very happy just playing ragtime. Maybe I would. I don't know. If I would probably maybe be getting paid enough for it, if I was in the right kind of a place and so forth, maybe I would be satisfied just to play ragtime. Or, as a lot of people say, Dixieland, I feel quite flattered when people come in and say, well, we've heard so much about you as a Dixieland jazz piano player, you know? Well, this is very flattering because, as I said before, there's no greater compliment to be paid you to say you are highly rated as a Dixieland musician.

Let's say this. Suppose that all commercial considerations were put aside, and you were given this club, and somebody would say, play anything you want, use whatever kind of a combo you want. What would you think would be the ideal kind of group you'd want to build? And what kind of music would you be playing?

I think if I was turned, if this club was turned over to me, and they'd say, now you put whatever you want in there, you play whatever you want, I think I would say, well, now maybe for one set, we're going to play a certain type of music, maybe 10 or 15 minutes of ragtime. And then maybe we'd come back the next set and say, well, now we're going to devote the next 15 minutes to some real good jazz. Or maybe we'll come back and play 15 minutes to something else. In other words, I don't think that I would particularly want to make it one particular type of music. I think it's good to play all types. Of course, it may be getting in a little bit of a commercial sort of a groove this way, but I think if you play good ragtime, Dixieland, even the good swing piano, the good swing era, maybe not just piano, but the swing era alone, you know, was a great era. And I think if you play all of this music and combine it and put it together, I mean, I think you've got some good music. And I don't think that it, I really believe that it can become tiresome listening to any particular one thing too long.
Right. Especially if you do have wider scope and you're not using your fullest abilities.

That's right. That's right. In other words, playing ragtime in Dixieland does not give you the full scope that you would really like to have. I mean, it doesn't give you the real full freedom of improvisation that you would like to have.

If I can focus for just a minute on a couple of questions pertinent to ragtime, do you think that ragtime is a dying art? Do you think that it's something that's bound to die out as the present experts become fewer and fewer in number like yourself? Do you think that it's a genre that's going to be submerged ultimately and disappear?

No, Charlie, I don't think it will disappear because there are too many people interested in it today. And there are too many jazz clubs throughout the country. For instance, California, you have clubs out there who are devoted entirely to this form of music. And I really don't think that it will ever completely die out because it's sort of something, a tradition, that people just don't want to let die.
Would this be too difficult to ask you in just a second, who do you consider to be, say, three of the greatest exponents of ragtime alive today?

Three of the greatest ragtime exponents alive today? Well, that's really a question, Charlie. I know there is a fellow by the name of Wally Rose who is considered a real great ragtime pianist. And then you have this Max Morath who has been on educational TV who really plays a real bang-up ragtime piano. And, well, I can't think just offhand, but there are several pianists around who are really playing real fine ragtime. I mean, they can, they really do a real good job. Okay.

Do you want to go back and play? Left off, let's see, we're talking about ragtime, this was kind of shifted a bit. You made many recordings in the past years. Do you have any sessions that you would point out to as being your favorite or your better sessions that you feel are more representative of your playing?

Yeah, the sessions that I made that are better representative are on Golden Crest label with, it's under the title of Rags and Blues. And then, of course, the records that I made with Ray Badouk, I think, on drums, that was just drum and piano solos, you know, when I made Little Rock Getaway. I made an album on Circle back in 1950 that was very good, technically, you know, I mean, from a recording standpoint and all.
Have you ever recorded anything which shows the broader scope of your playing? I just heard you're playing, was it, was it that Melchor May tune, was it? What were you just doing?
Cast Your Fate to the Wind?

Yeah, and then I've heard you do several other things that I think are excellent in that same vein, like Taste of Honey. Has this phase of your musical personality ever been recorded accurately, you think?

No, I don't believe accurately. I've tried to put it across on some of the recordings. The album that I made here at the Gollywog that has never been released, I think, contains more of this than anything else that I've ever done. But it's been most unfortunate that it's never been released. And in this album, I attempted more styles, different things that I've ever done before. In fact, I did a lot of Royal Heinz, Teddy Wilson, George Shearing, Jess Stacey, Errol Garner. In fact, I tried to cover practically every pianist of any importance that I could ever think of.

Mm-hmm. Speaking of records, what about records with bands where you function as a sideman, with any sessions that you think, either from your point of view or as a whole were more outstanding than others that you can think of offhand?
Well, I think some of the sessions that I made with Sharky were very good from a real Dixieland standpoint.
What label was that?
Well, that was the beginning of the revival of Dixieland around 1949. It was on a label called Bandwagon. That's Roger Wolfe. It was Roger Wolfe, the old disc jockey from WDSU. It was his label.

Okay. Now, I haven't been on the jazz scene very long, but ever since I've been on and I've been reading in jazz journals, it seems to me that you've, I've never seen a review that says anything bad about Alman Haugen. I've read the old jazz record magazine and Record Changer and Downbeat and Metronome. I really don't think that you ever had a negative review. It's a remarkable thing. Do you collect your clippings? Do you save these things? Yes.

I have tried to save most of them, Charlie, and some of them are very, very flattering and as you say, I've gotten some mighty good reviews. I think about the worst review that I ever received when you're talking about receiving bad ones was back in 1950. I cut some sides for Capital, Capital Recording Company was down there and they got a very bad setup to do it. They put up, they wanted to get an old honky-tonk style of piano and they had nothing to do with but to put an old chain across the keys, across the strings, you know, and the sound came out very cluttered up and very corny-like and Barry Ulenoff who was reviewing records in the metronome at that time, you know, he was really a tough critic, you know, and he got a hold of these recordings that I made and boy, did he pan them.
I remember correctly, I think that the A&R job was sort of leaning towards a commercial on that session too, wasn't it?

It was, yes, they wanted strictly commercial and we leaned more a little bit towards corny ragtime, you know, and of course Barry Ulenoff got this and this was supposed to be representative of true New Orleans Dixieland, you know, and he says, well, if this is what it is, he says, I don't want it, you see, so many people began writing him in and telling him that he was very wrong about his opinion of me as a pianist, that when he came to New Orleans, he made it a point to come to the Bayou Bar at the Pontchartrain Hotel and I recognized him by his pictures, you know, so I didn't say anything and I started turning on some progressive music for him, you know, some of the big spider back and some of the progressive music that I knew and I could see his face beaming, you know, when I got up, when I went over there, he called me, when I got up, he called me over, he says, I'm Barry Ulenoff, I said, yes, I knew, he said, you sound a lot different than you did on those records, see, so when he went back, he gave me a review again and he called me the greatest Dixieland pianist that he had heard in modern times and said that I was not only a great Dixieland pianist but a great modern pianist, so I thought that was quite flattering.

It seems like major labels so often take our bands and they dress them up and then they lose all the flavor, all the natural feeling that the groups and individuals actually project into their playing in the normal conditions. Remember when they got Hoda Sharky and made him do Pizza Pie Boogie and some other, Mickey Mouse, that's right, where the band was really great, you remember that band around 49, you were talking about, it was really wonderful and Capital lost the band when they tried to record commercials.

That's right, they started trying to make him record commercial but it just wasn't a real good commercial. This is a good point, Charlie, I think that when you do commercial, you have to really do it real good or either just let it alone.
Right. What do you think of the current Dixieland revival? Do you think it's a healthy thing, the thing that's centered around Preservation Hall?

I think that the revival of Dixieland around Preservation Hall has been most fortunate for these musicians who hadn't played for so long. It gave them a chance to really get some work and it brought them out and some of them are real good musicians. However, I don't believe that this is just truly representative of just New Orleans musicians because you have so many musicians who played jazz, you know, I mean, Dixieland jazz and I believe a lot of people today hear Preservation Hall and they completely forget about any other type of Dixieland music which I don't really, I really don't like too much. I mean, this course, this is my personal opinion and as I said before, I'm not criticizing Preservation Hall musicians because there are many good ones and I think in general and in a whole I think that it's good for New Orleans because I think when people come here they go down there and they say, well, this is New Orleans music but there are a lot of other, what I'm getting at is that there is a lot of other good New Orleans music around.

I think this brings to mind something else. It's kind of a confused tradition in New Orleans that's been brought up that the glorification of the older musicians by critics and by fans has often overemphasized the older Negro musicians. I think we had some rabid white musicians who'd complain about this like Nick Garaka in kind of extreme terms and it's been sort of a cluttered image that's been presented to the public. You as a person who understudied the earlier jazz musicians, colored and white, might be able to throw some light on this. Do you think that the revival at Preservation Hall and thereabouts is distorted, overemphasized, let's say, underplaying the role of the white musicians who were important in the beginnings of jazz?

Well, I'll put it the way Nick LaRocca put it, as you say. I think that the jazz music belongs to New Orleans. You hate to get into something where you say which was better, was the colored music better or the white jazz music better? I think that stuff stuff

music had its place where they had the marching bands, which was a definite, a particular style of New Orleans, which I think belonged entirely, mostly, to the to the to the colored people. However, I do believe this, that the white musicians brought jazz to a higher level, to a higher standard, in when they brought it to New York. For instance, Nick LaRocca always said this, that that when they went to New York with their band, they played a different type of jazz. In fact, if you listen to it, if you listen to Dixieland One Step and That's A Plenty, and the type of tunes that the original Dixieland jazz band made, it's entirely different from the style of music that the marching bands did. Now of course I'm not trying to get into any controversy as to which was better or which was worse, but I do say this, that a lot of people had neglected the white part of this music, thinking that the Negro music was the only type of music, but I don't believe that it was. Okay. Of course I might get on for this.

I think you have a good point, because look, for example, at the reputation, commercially speaking of George Lewis and Raymond Burke. Raymond in his own way is, seems to me, is fully great a jazz musician as George is.
Well, I think every bit, every bit, I would even go so far as to say that I think even greater in some respects.
Right. But George is, worldwide, I think George is better known. He's better known, that's right.
He's better known, that's right.
There's a New Orleans cult who knows Raymond, but it seems to be limited to those who have been here and have heard him, and who have truly an intensive view into the New Orleans scene.
If you get to work with Raymond Burke and get to know how he plays, you know that he is really outstanding, and I don't think that, well, I mean, there's not many that can come up to him.

Did you have anything you wanted to add, generally, to the content I brought out, or asked about, anything that you think is important in describing your playing, or your career, or any phase of it that I haven't learned more?

Well, I think, Charlie, that first of all, you really have to like what you're doing, which is most important. And I have liked music, I've liked jazz music all my life, been around many, many greats, and I feel quite flattered to be associated with these people. And I'm really, really proud of the reputation that I have around New Orleans as a Dixieland jazz piano player, or whatever they want to call me, ragtime. It's still jazz. And especially when they associate it with New Orleans, it's very flattering. And there's very little that I could add to it, excepting to say that I'm thankful that I'm still playing, that I've gone through the different phases, different styles, and that I'm still around.
Okay. Thanks a lot, Alvin.
Thank you. Thanks a lot. Thanks a lot. Thanks a lot.
